summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old woman was admitted with worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, and sharp chest pain over the prior three days, initially raising concern for reaccumulation of pericardial effusion. She had been hospitalized a month earlier for pericardial effusion of unknown etiology. Evaluation revealed new pulmonary venous congestion on chest X-ray and elevated proBNP, consistent with acute on chronic diastolic heart failure. There was no evidence of myocardial infarction, and bedside ultrasound showed no significant pericardial effusion. A repeat echocardiogram confirmed a small, stable pericardial effusion with no hemodynamic compromise. She was treated with increased furosemide dosing, which improved her symptoms and resolved pulmonary rales. A weakly positive urinalysis led to a short course of ciprofloxacin for asymptomatic UTI. She remained stable, was discharged home on increased diuresis, and advised to monitor weight and continue outpatient work-up for possible malignancy and shoulder pain.
